items.title: What Feeds Desire, and What Starves It: Eight Alluring Marks Against the Body's Own Impurity

items.zh: 此貪欲蓋以何為食？答：有淨妙相，及於彼相不正思惟多所修習，以之為食。淨妙相者，謂第一勝妙諸欲之相。若能於此遠離染心，於餘下劣亦得離染。如制強力，餘劣自伏。此復云何？謂女人身上八處所攝可愛淨相；由此八處，女縛於男。所謂歌、舞、笑、睇、美容、進止、妙觸、就禮。由此因緣，所有貪欲未生令生，生已增長，故名為食。問：
items.en: What feeds the hindrance of desire? Answer: An appealing appearance, together with sustained unsound reflection on it, is its food. What is this, specifically? It is the eight captivating features belonging to a woman's body, by which a woman binds a man — song, dance, smiling, a lingering glance, beauty of face, graceful bearing, soft touch, and physical union. Through these causes, desire not yet arisen is caused to arise, and once arisen, is caused to grow — this is why they are called its food.

items.zh: 此貪欲蓋誰為非食？答：有不淨相，及於彼相如理作意多所修習，以為非食。此復云何？謂青瘀等。若觀此身種種不淨雜穢充滿，名觀內身不淨之相；復觀於外青瘀等相種種不淨、名觀外身不淨之相。由觀此二不淨相故，未生貪欲令其不生，生已能斷，故名非食。
items.en: What starves the hindrance of desire? Answer: An impure appearance, together with sustained sound reflection on it, is what starves it. What is this, specifically? It is contemplating discoloration and the rest. Observing this very body as filled with every kind of impurity is called contemplating the inward body's impurity; observing outwardly the discoloration and other stages a corpse passes through is called contemplating the outward body's impurity. Through contemplating both these impurities, desire not yet arisen is prevented from arising, and once arisen, is severed — this is why they are called what starves it.

items.zh: 由於彼相如理作意故、遮令不生；多所修習故，生已能斷。前黑品中，由於彼相不正思惟故，未生令生；多所修習故、倍更增廣。問：

items.title: Nine Occasions for Anger, and Loving-Kindness as Its One Real Antidote

items.zh: 瞋恚蓋以何為食？答：有瞋恚性、有瞋恚相，及於彼相不正思惟多所修習，以之為食。依於種種不饒益事，心生惱害，名瞋恚性。不饒益事，名瞋恚相。於九惱事不正作意，名不正思惟。
items.en: What feeds the hindrance of ill will? Answer: An angry disposition, an angry appearance, and sustained unsound reflection on it are its food. Resting on various harmful matters, the mind's own arising urge to injure is called the angry disposition. The harmful deed itself is called the angry appearance. Unsound attention towards the nine occasions for resentment is called unsound reflection.

items.zh: 此瞋恚蓋誰為非食？答：有仁慈賢善，及於彼相如理作意、多所修習以為非食。又此慈善，恒欲與他安樂為相，修力所攝。由思擇力所攝作意，調伏九惱。以能斷除瞋恚蓋故，經中唯說此為非食。問：
items.en: What starves the hindrance of ill will? Answer: Genuine kindness and goodwill, together with sustained sound reflection on it, is what starves it. This kindness and goodwill is characterised by constantly wishing others well-being, sustained through the power of cultivation; and through the power of careful discernment, it subdues all nine occasions for resentment. Because it is capable of severing the hindrance of ill will, the sūtras name this alone as what starves it.

items.title: Three Kinds of Light Against Dullness: Starlight, the Dharma's Own Radiance, and a Deva's Body

items.zh: 惛沈睡眠蓋以何為食？答：有黑暗相，及於彼相不正思惟多所修習以之為食。問：此蓋誰為非食？答：有光明相，及於彼相如理作意多所修習，以為非食。明有三種。一、治暗光明，二、法光明，三、依身光明。
items.en: What feeds the hindrance of dullness and drowsiness? Answer: A darkened appearance, together with sustained unsound reflection on it, is its food. What starves this hindrance? Answer: A luminous appearance, together with sustained sound reflection on it, is what starves it. Light is of three kinds: light that counters literal darkness, the light of the Dharma, and light radiating from a being's own body.

items.zh: 治暗光明復有三種。一、在夜分，謂星月等；二、在晝分，謂日光明；三、在俱分，謂火珠等。法光明者：謂如有一，隨其所受、所思、所觸，觀察諸法；或復修習隨念佛等。依身光明者，謂諸有情自然身光。
items.en: Light countering literal darkness is of three further kinds: by night, starlight and moonlight; by day, sunlight; and at either time, firelight or a luminous gem. The light of the Dharma is this: observing all phenomena resting on what one has learned, reflected on, and directly experienced of the teaching; or, further, cultivating recollection of the Buddha and the rest. Light radiating from the body is the natural radiance certain beings' own bodies give off.

items.zh: 當知初明治三種暗。一者、夜暗，二者、雲暗，三者、障暗。謂窟宅等。法明能治三種黑暗。由不如實知諸法故，於去來今多生疑惑，於佛法等亦復如是。此中無明及疑，俱名黑暗。又證觀察能治惛沈睡眠黑暗，以能顯了諸法性故。問：

items.title: What Feeds Restlessness: Family, Homeland, the Illusion of Endless Time, and Remembered Pleasure

items.zh: 掉舉惡作蓋以何為食？答：於親屬等所有尋思、於曾所經戲笑等念、及於彼相不正思惟多所修習，以之為食。親屬尋思者，謂因親屬或盛或衰、或離或合，發欣慼行，心生籌慮等。國土尋思者，謂因國土盛衰等相，廣如前說。不死尋思者，謂因少年及衰老位諸有所作或利他事，發欣慼行，心生籌慮等。
items.en: What feeds the hindrance of restlessness and remorse? Answer: Thoughts of family and the rest, memories of past laughter and amusement, together with sustained unsound reflection on them, are its food. Thoughts of family are these: prompted by a family member's prosperity or decline, separation or reunion, gladness or grief arises, and the mind churns over it at length. Thoughts of homeland are these: prompted by a homeland's own prosperity or decline. Thoughts of freedom from imminent death are these: prompted by what one could still accomplish, for oneself or others, in youth or in old age, gladness or grief arises, and the mind churns over it at length.

items.zh: 笑者，謂隨有一，或因開論、或因合論，現齒而笑，歡聚啞啞。戲者，謂雙陸、摴蒱、弄珠等戲。或有所餘種類歡樂。謂互相受用，受用境界，受諸快樂；或由同處，或因戲論，歡娛而住。所行事者，謂相執持手臂髮等，或相摩觸隨一身分，或抱或嗚，或相顧眄，或作餘事。問：
items.en: Laughter is this: through elaborate storytelling or talk that draws comparisons, teeth bared in laughter, a joyful gathering's noise. Games are this: dice, gambling, and similar amusements. There are, further, other kinds of pleasure: mutual enjoyment between people, and enjoyment of sensory objects, each bringing its own pleasure. Physical intimacy is this: holding hands or hair, touching any part of the body, embracing, kissing, exchanging lingering glances, or other such acts.

blocks.text: The Buddha taught that each hindrance has its "food" (食), what nourishes it, and its "non-food", what starves it. Today the treatise works through four of the five. This passage is one of the most practical meditation instructions in the early Buddhist tradition, and the treatise expands it carefully.

subs.head: Desire: fed by attractive marks, starved by unattractiveness

blocks.text: Desire is fed by **attractive marks** and unsound attention to them: eight alluring features of the body, such as complexion, shape, touch, and gesture. It is starved by "an impure appearance, together with sustained sound reflection on it": contemplating the body's inner impurity and, outwardly, the stages of a corpse's discolouration.

Venerable Miào Jìng on method: "the wisdom of observation must be repeated again and again; fearing repetition won't work." The point is not disgust but correction: desire exaggerates one aspect of the body; the contemplation restores the rest.

subs.head: Ill will: fed by nine resentments, starved by kindness

blocks.text: Ill will is fed by unsound attention to **nine occasions for resentment**: someone has harmed, is harming, or will harm me; or those I love; or has helped, is helping, or will help those I dislike. It is starved by **loving-kindness** (慈). The sūtras name kindness alone as its remedy.

Master Cháng Bǎi's advice: "If you're often very angry at someone, learn to practise loving-kindness towards that very person, wishing them well; gradually the anger ends." The remedy is aimed at the specific person, not at beings in general.

Dullness and drowsiness are fed by heaviness, fatigue, and unsound attention to darkness. They are starved by the **perception of light**: physical light (starlight, the sun, a lamp); the light of the Dharma ("observing all phenomena through what one has learned, reflected on, and directly experienced of the teaching", or recollecting the Buddha); and the light of a deva's body. Master Cháng Bǎi quotes the *Platform Sūtra*: one moment of wisdom is like a lamp that ends a thousand years of darkness.
Venerable Miào Jìng adds that impurity contemplation, loving-kindness, and breath mindfulness can also count as "perceptions of light": anything that brightens and steadies the mind.

Restlessness and remorse are fed by thoughts of family, homeland, and "**not dying**" (the illusion of endless time), and by remembering past pleasures. Venerable Miào Jìng describes it: feeling "I'll live at least two thousand years", not sensing that one missed breath ends it all; energetic for chores, tired for practice.

The remedy, in tomorrow's reading, is calm. For now, notice the diagnosis: much restlessness in meditation is the mind refusing to accept that time is short. Remembering death is not morbid here; it is the cure for distraction.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what starves the hindrance of desire?
options: the impure appearance with sustained sound reflection — contemplating inner bodily impurity and outer discoloration
quiz.why: "An impure appearance, together with sustained sound reflection on it, is what starves it. … It is contemplating discoloration and the rest." Master Cháng Bǎi cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: impure things fill the body, leaking endlessly like a torn bag.

quiz.q: In impurity contemplation, what does Venerable Miào Jìng say about the observing wisdom?
options: it must be repeated again and again — fearing repetition won't do
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Observing it as false, the wisdom of observation must be repeated again and again; fearing repetition won't work." The text's "sustained" reflection means repeated practice.

quiz.q: Unsound attention to "nine occasions for resentment" feeds ill will. How are the nine counted?
options: oneself, those one loves, those one dislikes — three; plus past, future, present, each for enemies and friends — six more
self plus loved and disliked across three times
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The latter three — enemy and friend — each split into two, making nine occasions for resentment in all." Venerable Miào Jìng: "Enemy and friend two each across three times — six — plus the earlier three." The reading note's 1+3+3 yields only seven (logged).

quiz.q: The sūtras name kindness alone as what starves ill will. What does Master Cháng Bǎi advise if one is often angry at someone?
options: practice loving-kindness towards that very person, wishing them well, gradually ending the anger
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "If you're often very angry at someone, learn to practise loving-kindness towards them, wishing them well — gradually the anger is cut." The text: kindness constantly wishes others well-being and, through discernment, subdues all nine occasions.

quiz.q: The luminous appearance starves dullness. What is the light of the Dharma, and what saying does Master Cháng Bǎi cite?
options: observing phenomena through what one has learned, reflected on, and experienced, or recollecting the Buddha — citing the Platform Sūtra: "one lamp dispels a thousand years' darkness"
quiz.why: "Observing all phenomena resting on what one has learned, reflected on, and directly experienced of the teaching; or … recollection of the Buddha." Master Cháng Bǎi: the *Platform Sūtra* says one lamp dispels a thousand years' darkness. Venerable Miào Jìng: received is hearing, reflected is thought, touched is realisation.

quiz.q: "Thoughts of not dying" feed restlessness. How does Venerable Miào Jìng describe this in people?
options: feeling "I'll live at least two thousand years," not sensing one breath could end it — energetic for chores, tired for practice
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Feeling 'I'll live at least two thousand years!' — not sensing that if one breath fails, you're dead"; busy with chores you're full of energy, but for practice "I'm tired, my back hurts!" The text: thinking of what one could still do in youth or age.
